lessons.title: Letters & Sounds
objectives: Know the 19 letters used in Hiligaynon
Say one example word for each letter

parts.title: Meet Hiligaynon
parts.text: Hiligaynon, also called Ilonggo, is spoken by around 9 million people, mostly in Iloilo, Capiz, Guimaras and Negros Occidental. Many Ilonggo families also live outside the Visayas, including here in Sta. Maria, Sto. Tomas. It is a Visayan language, so it is related to Cebuano and Kinaray-a, and it shares many words with Filipino.

parts.title: Letters You Already Know
parts.text: Hiligaynon is written with the same alphabet as Filipino, so you can already read it. Native Hiligaynon words use only *19 letters*. Letters like C, F, J, Q, V, X and Z show up only in borrowed words and names, like *Jose* and *Cebu*.

parts.title: “NG” Is One Letter
parts.text: Just like in Filipino, *ng* is one sound, the ng in “sing”. In Hiligaynon it often starts a word, so practise saying it at the beginning.

parts.title: The Short Stop (-)
parts.text: A hyphen inside a word means a short stop in your throat, like the catch in “uh-oh”. Say *gab-i* as gab–i, not gabi. Skipping the stop makes the word sound Tagalog.

parts.prompt: Which word has a short stop in the middle?
parts.explain: The hyphen in gab-i shows the short stop.

parts.title: Read Your First Words
parts.tip: Don't worry about the meaning yet. Read each line aloud and copy the audio. You'll learn these words in the next lessons.

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: The letters sound the same as in Filipino, so reading is easy.
The vowel *o* often sounds between o and u: *anom* can sound like “anum”.
Stress can change a word's meaning, so copy the audio, not just the spelling.

letters.name: o
letters.soundHint: between o in "go" and u in "put"

letters.name: ra
letters.soundHint: a quick tap, like Spanish r

lessons.note: No quiz. Finishing all 19 letters unlocks Lesson 2. If the app's Alphabet module already shows these cards, link to it instead of duplicating.

lessons.title: Greetings & Courtesy
objectives: Greet people at any time of day
Use polite words like please and thank you

parts.title: Greetings by Time of Day
parts.text: Hiligaynon greetings use *Maayong* (“good”) plus the time of day, just like *Magandang* in Filipino.

parts.prompt: It's 8 in the evening and your neighbor walks by. What do you say?

parts.title: Asking “How Are You?”
parts.text: *Kamusta ka?* comes from Spanish “¿cómo está?”, just like Filipino *Kumusta*. Answer with *Maayo man ako*, then ask back with *Ikaw man?* The little word *man* works like *naman*.

parts.title: Polite Words
parts.text: These four small words make you sound kind and respectful. Ilonggo is often called a soft, sweet-sounding (*malambing*) language, and polite words are a big part of that.

parts.prompt: Someone says “Salamat!” to you. What do you reply?

parts.title: Greeting an Older Neighbor
parts.setting: Ana meets Manang Rosa on the street in the afternoon.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.fil: Mabuti naman, salamat. Kumusta po kayo?

parts.tip: Hiligaynon has no *po* or *opo*. Ana shows respect by calling her *Manang* and asking *Kamusta kamo?* (kayo) instead of *Kamusta ka?*

parts.title: A Thank-You Message
parts.tip: This short message uses a greeting, thanks and an apology, all from this lesson. *Halong!* means take care.

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: *Maayong* = *Magandang*. Put the time of day after it.
*Kamusta ka?* = *Kumusta ka?* Only one letter changes.
*man* works like *naman*: Maayo *man* ako = Mabuti *naman* ako.
*Palihog* goes at the start of a request: *Palihog*, hulata ako = *Paki*hintay ako.

mistakes.why: Don't mix Filipino and Hiligaynon in one greeting.

parts.title: Did you know?
parts.text: Hiligaynon has no *po* or *opo*. Ilonggos show respect by calling older people *Manang* or *Nang* (older woman) and *Manong* or *Nong* (older man), and by speaking in a soft, polite tone.

example.hil: Maayo man ako, salamat. Ikaw man?
example.fil: Mabuti naman ako, salamat. Ikaw naman?

questions.source: B1-5 (changed to Filipino -> Hiligaynon to match Figma)

questions.situation: You meet your Lola in the morning. How do you greet her?

questions.prompt: In the conversation, why does Ana say “Kamusta kamo?” to Manang Rosa?
options: To be polite to an older person

lessons.title: Pronouns & Identity
objectives: Use the words for I, you, he and she

parts.title: Words for People
parts.text: Like Filipino, Hiligaynon pronouns don't show if someone is male or female. *Siya* means he or she. Use *ikaw* at the start of a sentence and the short *ka* after another word.

parts.title: Two Words for “We”
parts.text: *Kami* leaves the listener out. *Kita* includes the listener. It's the same idea as *kami* and *tayo* in Filipino, so choose carefully when you invite someone.

parts.explain: Kita includes the listener, like tayo.

parts.title: Saying “My”
parts.text: Put *ko* after the thing: *balay ko*. Or put *akon* before it, with *nga*: *akon nga balay*. Both mean *bahay ko*.

parts.title: Ana's Class

lines.hil: Si Ma'am Rosa ang amon manunudlo.
lines.fil: Si Ma'am Rosa ang aming guro.

parts.tip: Ana says *amon* (aming) about her class, but *kita* (tayo) when she invites you.

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: In Filipino, “mahal *kita*” uses kita for “you”. In Hiligaynon, *kita* means “we, you and me”.
Like Filipino, the describing word comes first: *Manunudlo siya* = *Guro siya*.

mistakes.wrong: Kadto kami sa merkado. (inviting a friend)
mistakes.why: Use kita when the listener is included.
akon goes before the noun, with nga.

parts.title: Did you know?
parts.text: Ilonggos often invite anyone nearby to share food with *Kaon ta!* (Kain tayo!). *Ta* is the short form of *kita*.

questions.source: B2-2 (replaced: 'akon balay' is common in casual speech)

questions.situation: You want your friend to come with you to the market. What do you say?

questions.source: B2-4 (replaced: answer was the same in Filipino)

questions.prompt: In “Ana's Class”, why does Ana say “Kadto kita” and not “Kadto kami”?
options: She is inviting you to come too
She is talking about her teacher

lessons.title: Introducing Yourself
objectives: Say where you are from and your age
Talk about your work or study

parts.title: Your Name
parts.text: *Ngalan* means *pangalan*, the same word without *pa-*. The easiest way to give your name is *Ako si ___*.

parts.title: Where You Are From: Taga-
parts.text: *Taga-* plus a place means “from that place”, exactly like in Filipino.

parts.prompt: How do you say you're from Sto. Tomas?

parts.title: Age and Work
parts.text: *Pila* means “how many”. For age, Ilonggos often use Spanish-based numbers, like *baynte* (20) and *trenta* (30).

parts.title: Keep the Talk Going
parts.text: End your answer with *Ikaw man?* (Ikaw naman?) so the other person can introduce themselves too.

parts.title: Meeting a New Classmate
parts.setting: Ana meets Ben on the first day of class.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.hil: Maayong aga! Ako si Ana. Ano ang imo ngalan?
lines.fil: Magandang umaga! Ako si Ana. Ano ang pangalan mo?

parts.tip: *diri* means *dito*. You'll learn more place words in Lesson 8.

parts.title: Ben Introduces Himself

lines.hil: Estudyante ako. Nagaeskwela ako diri sa Sto. Tomas.
lines.fil: Estudyante ako. Nag-aaral ako rito sa Sto. Tomas.

lines.hil: Ikaw man? Ano ang imo ngalan?
lines.fil: Ikaw naman? Ano ang pangalan mo?

parts.tip: Ben uses all four steps from this lesson: name, age, hometown, and work or study.

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: *Imo* comes before the noun (*imo ngalan*); *mo* comes after (*ngalan mo*). Both mean “your”.

mistakes.why: Use the short ka after the question word.

parts.title: Did you know?
parts.text: Ilonggos often ask *Taga-diin ka?* soon after meeting someone. Knowing a person's hometown is a friendly way to connect.

example.hil: Ano ang imo trabaho? Nars ako.
example.fil: Ano ang trabaho mo? Nars ako.

questions.prompt: In "Pila ka tuig ka na?", what is the FIRST "ka"?
options: The word that links a number to a noun

questions.source: B3-4 (changed: answer was the same in Filipino)

questions.situation: A new classmate asks you, "Ano ang imo ngalan?" What do you reply?

questions.prompt: In the conversation, where is Ben from?

questions.modelAnswer: Maayong aga! Ako si Ana. Taga-Batangas ako. Estudyante ako. Ikaw man?
questions.hint: Write one or two sentences. Any answer is accepted.

parts.title: Counting 1 to 10
parts.text: Many Hiligaynon numbers are the same as Filipino. Watch out for three that are different: *duha*, *anom* and *napulo*.

parts.title: Counting Things: Number + ka
parts.text: Filipino joins a number and a thing with *-ng* or *na* (dalawa*ng* bata). Hiligaynon always puts *ka* in the middle.

parts.title: Two Number Systems
parts.text: For prices, age and time, Ilonggos often use Spanish-based numbers. For counting things, use the native numbers.

parts.title: At the Sari-sari Store

lines.hil: May tatlo ka itlog sa lamesa.

parts.tip: *Tagpila?* means *Magkano?* You'll use it a lot in Lesson 9.

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: *tatlo, apat, lima, pito, walo* and *siyam* are the same in both languages.

mistakes.why: Use one number system at a time.

parts.title: Did you know?
parts.text: For prices, age and time, Ilonggos often use Spanish-based numbers like *baynte* (20) and *trenta* (30).

questions.source: B4-3 (changed: tens are not in this lesson)

questions.situation: At the store, you want three eggs. What do you say?

questions.prompt: In “At the Sari-sari Store”, how many eggs are on the table?

parts.title: Day and Sun, Month and Moon
parts.text: Hiligaynon uses one word for day and sun (*adlaw*) and one for month and moon (*bulan*), just like Filipino *araw* and *buwan*. Watch out for *simana*: it means a week, not Sunday.

parts.title: Days of the Week
parts.text: The days come from Spanish, so most look like Filipino. The big difference is Sunday: *Domingo*.

parts.explain: Sunday is Domingo. Simana means a week.

parts.title: Months of the Year
parts.text: Months also come from Spanish and are almost the same as Filipino.

parts.title: Today, Tomorrow, Yesterday
parts.text: These words tell you when something happens. *Kahapon* is the same as Filipino, but *ngayon* and *bukas* are different.

parts.title: Telling the Time
parts.text: Use *alas-* with a Spanish number, then *sang* and the part of the day. For 1 o'clock, say *ala-una*.

parts.prompt: How do you say 7:00 in the morning?
parts.explain: Use alas- with the Spanish number siyete, then sang aga.

parts.title: Ana's Week

lines.hil: Kada Lunes, may klase si Ana sa aga.
lines.fil: Tuwing Lunes, may klase si Ana sa umaga.

lines.hil: Buwas Martes. Magkadto siya sa merkado.
lines.fil: Bukas ay Martes. Pupunta siya sa palengke.

lines.hil: Sa Sabado, wala siya sing klase.

parts.tip: *kahapon* goes with *nag-* actions (done) and *buwas* goes with *mag-* actions (later). You'll learn these in Lesson 10.

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: In time, Filipino *ng* = Hiligaynon *sang*: alas-tres *ng* hapon = alas-tres *sang* hapon.

parts.title: Did you know?
parts.text: To greet someone on their birthday, say *Malipayon nga Kaadlawan!* (Maligayang kaarawan!). *Kaadlawan* comes from *adlaw*, day.

example.hil: Sang Sabado nagkadto kami sa merkado.
example.fil: Noong Sabado pumunta kami sa palengke.

questions.prompt: In “Ana's Week”, what day is it today?

lessons.title: Family & People
objectives: Use respectful terms like Manang and Manong

parts.title: Your Close Family
parts.text: Hiligaynon has its own words for mother and father, *iloy* and *amay*, but *nanay* and *tatay* are used every day too. *Utod* means a brother or sister, and *manghod* is a younger one.

parts.title: Your Extended Family
parts.text: *Lolo*, *lola*, *tiyo* and *tiya* are the same as Filipino. Cousins, nephews and nieces use different words.

parts.title: Calling People Respectfully
parts.text: Hiligaynon has no *po* or *opo*. Instead, Ilonggos show respect by how they call people.

parts.title: Whose Is It?
parts.text: For a person's name, use *ni*: *ang iloy ni Ana*. For “my”, put *ko* after the word: *ang iloy ko*.

parts.title: This Is My Family

lines.hil: Si Rosa ang akon iloy kag si Jose ang akon amay.
lines.fil: Si Rosa ang aking nanay at si Jose ang aking tatay.
Si Ben ang aking nakababatang kapatid.

lines.hil: Taga-Batangas kami, pero taga-Iloilo ang akon lola.
lines.fil: Taga-Batangas kami, pero taga-Iloilo ang aking lola.

parts.tip: *kag* means *at* (and). *pero* is the same as Filipino.

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: Like Lesson 3: *aton nga pamilya* includes the listener; *amon nga pamilya* does not.

mistakes.why: Use Manang for an older woman.

parts.title: Did you know?
parts.text: Ilonggos often call older neighbors *Tiya*, *Tiyo*, *Manang* or *Manong*, even if they are not relatives.

example.fil: Si Ben ang aking nakababatang kapatid.

items.note: hinablos (nephew/niece) is from general Hiligaynon knowledge; no online source was reachable to confirm it.

questions.situation: You meet your friend's older sister. What do you call her?

questions.prompt: In “This Is My Family”, who is Ben?

parts.title: Places in Town
parts.text: Many place words are the same as Filipino. The market is *merkado* and the road is *dalan*.

parts.title: This, That, Here, There
parts.text: Like Filipino *ito / iyan / iyon*, Hiligaynon has three distances.

parts.title: Saying Where: Ara sa
parts.text: *Ara sa* means *nasa* (is at). If someone is not there, use *wala*: *Wala si Nanay diri.*

parts.title: Directions
parts.text: Surprise: in Hiligaynon, *wala* means left and *tuo* means right. *Wala* also means “none”, so listen to the words around it.

terms.note: stop here (in a jeep or tricycle)

parts.title: Asking the Way
parts.setting: Ana asks a tricycle driver how to get to the market in Sto. Tomas.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.hil: Maayong aga, Nong! Diin ang merkado?
lines.fil: Magandang umaga po, Kuya! Saan ang palengke?

lines.speaker: Driver
lines.hil: Diretso lang, dayon liko sa tuo.

lines.speaker: Driver
lines.hil: Indi, malapit lang. Ara sa tupad sang simbahan.
lines.fil: Hindi, malapit lang. Nasa tabi ng simbahan.

parts.tip: *Nong* is a short, polite way to call an older man, like *Kuya*. *bala* works like *ba*.

parts.title: My Town

lines.hil: Malapit sa plasa ang amon balay.
lines.fil: Malapit sa plasa ang aming bahay.

lines.hil: Ang simbahan ara sa atubang sang plasa.
lines.fil: Nasa harap ng plasa ang simbahan.

lines.hil: Ang eskwelahan ara sa tupad sang simbahan.
lines.fil: Nasa tabi ng simbahan ang paaralan.

lines.hil: Sa merkado: diretso lang, dayon liko sa wala.
lines.fil: Papunta sa palengke: diretso lang, tapos kumaliwa.

parts.tip: *sa atubang sang* = *sa harap ng*; *sa tupad sang* = *sa tabi ng*.

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: For “behind”, you'll hear both *sa likod sang* and *sa luyo sang*.

parts.title: Did you know?
parts.text: In many towns, people give directions from the *plasa* (town plaza) and the *simbahan* (church), because almost everyone knows where they are.

example.hil: Ara ang tindahan sa tupad sang eskwelahan.
example.fil: Nasa tabi ng paaralan ang tindahan.

questions.prompt: In directions, what does “sa wala” mean?

questions.situation: You want the tricycle driver to turn right. What do you say?

questions.prompt: In the conversation, where is the market?

parts.title: Meals of the Day
parts.text: Each meal has its own word. *Paniudto* comes from *udto* (noon) and *panihapon* from *hapon* (afternoon).

parts.title: Kan-on or Bugas?
parts.text: Hiligaynon has two words for rice: *kan-on* is cooked rice and *bugas* is uncooked rice. *Sud-an* is the dish you eat with rice.

parts.title: How Does It Taste?
parts.text: *Namit* (or *manamit*) is the word you'll hear most at the table.

parts.title: Asking for Something
parts.text: Where Filipino uses *ng*, Hiligaynon uses *sang*.

parts.title: Asking the Price
parts.text: *Tagpila?* asks the price of each item. *Pila tanan?* asks for the total. At the market, prices are usually said with Spanish-based numbers.

parts.title: At the Palengke
parts.setting: Ana buys mangoes at the market.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.hil: Maayong aga, Nang. Tagpila ang mangga?
lines.fil: Magandang umaga po, Ate. Magkano ang mangga?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.hil: Mahal gid! Pwede kwarenta na lang?
lines.fil: Ang mahal! Puwede kuwarenta na lang?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.hil: Sige, duha ka kilo. Pila tanan?

parts.tip: Friendly bargaining is normal at the palengke. *Mahal gid!* is a polite way to ask for a lower price.

parts.title: Lunch at Home

lines.hil: Ang amon sud-an isda kag utan.
lines.fil: Isda at gulay ang aming ulam.

parts.tip: When the food is ready, you'll hear *Kaon ta!* (Kain tayo!).

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: *ng* = *sang*: Gusto ko *ng* tubig = Gusto ko *sang* tubig.

parts.title: Did you know?
parts.text: Ilonggo food is famous across the Philippines. *La Paz batchoy* and *pancit Molo* are both named after districts of Iloilo City.

example.hil: Kan-on kag itlog ang amon pamahaw.
example.fil: Kanin at itlog ang aming almusal.

questions.situation: Your friend's mother serves you lunch, and it tastes great. What do you say?

questions.prompt: In “At the Palengke”, how much does Ana pay in all?

questions.hint: Write one or two sentences. Any answer is accepted.
questions.modelAnswer: Maayong udto! Gusto ko sang kan-on kag isda, palihog. Tagpila tanan?

lessons.title: Basic Verbs
objectives: Say what you are doing, did and will do

parts.title: The Root Stays, the Start Changes
parts.text: English changes the word itself (eat, ate). Hiligaynon keeps the root, like *kaon* (eat), and changes the start: *naga-* for now, *nag-* for done, *mag-* for later.

parts.title: Now, Done, Later
parts.text: Read across: the root never changes.

parts.title: Who Did What
parts.text: The action comes first, then who does it, then *sang* and the thing.

parts.title: Telling Someone What to Do
parts.text: For a friendly command, just use the root: *Kaon na!* Add *ta* for “let's”: *Kaon ta!* To say “don't”, start with *Ayaw*.

parts.title: Ana's Day

lines.hil: Kahapon, nagkadto si Ana sa merkado.
lines.fil: Kahapon, pumunta si Ana sa palengke.

lines.hil: Nagpalit siya sang isda kag utan.
lines.fil: Bumili siya ng isda at gulay.

parts.tip: Look at the start of each action word: *nag-* (kahapon), *naga-* (subong), *mag-* (buwas).

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: The root never changes; only the start does.

mistakes.why: Use nag- for something already done.

parts.title: Did you know?
parts.text: When you visit an Ilonggo home, you may hear *Pasulod!* (Pasok!) and *Pungko anay!* (Upo ka muna!).

questions.prompt: In “Ana's Day”, what did Ana buy yesterday?

lessons.title: Asking Questions
objectives: Ask who, what, where and when

parts.title: Question Words
parts.text: Most question words look like Filipino with a small change. Three are new: *diin*, *san-o* and *ngaa*.

parts.title: Yes or No?
parts.text: Add *bala* (like *ba*) to make a yes-or-no question. Answer with *Huo* (yes) or *Indi* (no). For “not yet”, say *Wala pa*.

parts.title: Building a Question
parts.text: Start with the question word, then *ang* and the thing you are asking about.

parts.title: Getting to Know a Neighbor
parts.setting: Ana's new neighbor, Manang Lita, asks her some questions.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.hil: Ako si Ana, Nang. Bag-o lang kami diri.
lines.fil: Ako si Ana, Ate. Bago lang kami rito.

parts.tip: *Day* (from *Inday*) is a friendly way to call a young woman.

parts.title: Questions Ana Asks
parts.tip: Every question starts with the question word, just like in Filipino.

mistakes.why: Huo is the Hiligaynon word for yes.
ngaa (why) is not nga (the joining word).

parts.title: Did you know?
parts.text: *Nagkaon ka na?* (Kumain ka na?) is often used as a greeting. It shows that you care, more than a real question about food.

questions.situation: Someone asks “Nagkaon ka na bala?” You haven't eaten yet. What do you say?

questions.prompt: In the conversation, how many people live in Ana's house?

lessons.title: Building Sentences
objectives: Put words in the right order

parts.title: The Describing Word Comes First
parts.text: Most Hiligaynon sentences start with the description or the action, then who or what it is about. Filipino does this too.

parts.title: Small Marker Words
parts.text: These little words show each word's job in the sentence.

parts.title: Joining with nga
parts.text: Where Filipino adds *-ng* or *na*, Hiligaynon puts *nga* as a separate word.

parts.explain: Use nga to join a describing word to a thing.

parts.title: Saying No: indi, wala, ayaw
parts.text: This is the trickiest part for Filipino speakers: *hindi* splits into *indi* and *wala*.
rows: Indi ako doktor. / Indi ako magkadto.
Wala ako nagkaon. / Wala ako sing kwarta.

parts.title: Not Today

lines.hil: Indi ako magkadto sa eskwelahan subong.
lines.fil: Hindi ako pupunta sa paaralan ngayon.

lines.hil: Ayaw kabalaka, Nay. Magpalit lang ako.
lines.fil: Huwag kang mag-alala, Nay. Bibili lang ako.

parts.tip: *indi* for what you won't do, *wala* for what didn't happen or isn't there, *ayaw* for “don't”.

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: *hindi* = *indi* (is not, will not) or *wala* (did not, none).

mistakes.why: For something that didn't happen, use wala.
Write nga as a separate word.

questions.prompt: In “Not Today”, why is the speaker hungry?

lessons.title: Daily Conversations
objectives: Ask someone to repeat or slow down

parts.title: The Shape of a Conversation
parts.text: Most everyday talks follow five steps: greet, answer and ask back, the main topic, confirm, then say goodbye. You already know the first two from Lesson 2.

parts.title: When You Don't Understand
parts.text: It's normal not to catch everything. These phrases help you keep talking in Hiligaynon instead of switching to Filipino.

parts.prompt: How do you ask someone to speak slowly?

parts.title: Saying Goodbye
parts.text: *Halong!* (take care) is the warmest Ilonggo goodbye. Add *Asta sa liwat!* for “see you again”.

parts.title: Meeting a Neighbor
parts.setting: Ana meets Manang Lita on the way to the market.

lines.speaker: Manang Lita
lines.hil: Maayong hapon man. Diin ka makadto?
lines.fil: Magandang hapon din. Saan ka pupunta?

parts.title: Buying a Drink
parts.setting: Ana buys water at a sari-sari store.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.hil: Maayong aga. Gusto ko sang tubig, palihog.
lines.fil: Magandang umaga. Gusto ko po ng tubig.

parts.title: Asking for Help
parts.setting: Ana asks a man on the street for the hospital.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.hil: Pasayloa ako, Nong. Diin ang ospital?
lines.fil: Paumanhin po, Kuya. Saan ang ospital?

lines.speaker: Man
lines.hil: Sa sunod nga dalan, liko sa wala.
lines.fil: Sa susunod na kalye, kumaliwa ka.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.hil: Wala ko nahangpan. Hinay-hinay lang, palihog.
lines.fil: Hindi ko naintindihan. Dahan-dahan lang po.

parts.tip: Ana didn't switch to Filipino. She asked the man to slow down.

parts.title: Ana's Day in Sta. Maria

lines.hil: Kada aga, nagakadto ako sa merkado.
lines.fil: Tuwing umaga, pumupunta ako sa palengke.

lines.hil: Nagapalit ako sang isda kag utan.
lines.fil: Bumibili ako ng isda at gulay.

lines.hil: Sa hapon, nagabasa ako sang libro.
lines.fil: Sa hapon, nagbabasa ako ng libro.

parts.tip: This reading uses words from almost every lesson. How many do you know?

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: Plan your sentence in Filipino if it helps, then build it in Hiligaynon.
Hiligaynon has no *po* or *opo*. Use *Nang*, *Nong* and a polite tone.

mistakes.why: Ask the person to slow down instead.

parts.title: Did you know?
parts.text: Ilonggo speech is often called *malambing*: sweet and gentle. Speaking slowly and softly is part of being polite.

questions.situation: Someone talks too fast and you didn't understand. What do you say first?

questions.prompt: In “Buying a Drink”, how much is the water?
Say goodbye to a neighbor in Hiligaynon
questions.hint: Write one or two sentences. Any answer is accepted.
questions.modelAnswer: Salamat, Nang! Sige, lakat na ako. Halong! Asta sa liwat!
